summary: The chapter orders Israel's sacred calendar around weekly Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread, two harvest presentations linked by a commanded fifty-day count, a trumpet memorial, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Booths. Work stoppage, assembly, offerings, harvest restraint, self-denial, rejoicing, and temporary shelters give each appointed time its particular shape.
whyItMatters: The calendar makes holiness a recurring pattern in communal time. Worship, agricultural seasons, food shared with others, and remembrance of the exodus are held together through distinct observances.

context.author: Leviticus presents Yahweh giving the calendar to Moses; the finished book does not name its narrator, and its composition history remains debated.
context.audience: The children of Israel, who proclaim assemblies, stop ordinary work, bring produce and offerings, and keep the feasts across generations.
context.date: The calendar is narrated at Sinai and anticipates harvest in the land; the date of the book's received literary form is debated.
context.setting: Israel's future annual cycle in the land, with observance in households and holy convocations connected to sanctuary offerings.
context.literaryForm: A liturgical calendar organized by dates, repeated speech units, commanded assemblies, rest, and offerings.

outline.heading: Sabbath and the appointed-feast heading
outline.note: The weekly day of solemn rest opens the calendar before the annual dates are listed.

outline.heading: Passover and Unleavened Bread
outline.note: The first-month observances include a seven-day period bracketed by holy convocations.

outline.heading: The first sheaf and the fifty-day count
outline.note: Two harvest presentations, their animal and grain offerings, and the gleaning command connect worship with the land's produce.

outline.heading: A seventh-month trumpet memorial
outline.note: The month's first day is a solemn rest and holy convocation marked by trumpet blowing.

outline.heading: The Day of Atonement
outline.note: The tenth day requires self-denial and complete rest from evening to evening under severe penalties.

outline.heading: Booths, rejoicing, and the calendar declared
outline.note: Seven days plus an eighth-day assembly combine offerings, rest, branches, rejoicing, and temporary shelters recalling the exodus.

keyVerses.text: “‘Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, a holy convocation; you shall do no kind of work. It is a Sabbath to Yahweh in all your dwellings.
keyVerses.why: Weekly Sabbath opens the calendar with complete rest and a sacred assembly.

keyVerses.text: “‘When you reap the harvest of your land, you must not wholly reap into the corners of your field. You must not gather the gleanings of your harvest. You must leave them for the poor and for the foreigner. I am Yahweh your God.’”
keyVerses.why: Harvest celebration includes leaving produce for poor people and foreigners.

keyVerses.text: that your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in temporary shelters when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.’”
keyVerses.why: The chapter explains the booths as a way to remember Israel’s departure from Egypt.

questions.question: What is a holy convocation?
questions.answer: It is a proclaimed sacred assembly. The phrase recurs at the opening and on particular feast days, usually alongside a command to stop regular work and, in several cases, to present offerings before Yahweh.

questions.question: Why does weekly Sabbath appear in a list of annual feasts?
questions.answer: The chapter places the recurring seventh-day rest before the dated annual observances and calls it a holy convocation in every dwelling. That positioning makes weekly rest the first rhythm of holy time rather than an unrelated interruption to the festival calendar.

questions.question: What does this chapter itself say about Passover and Unleavened Bread?
questions.answer: It dates Passover to the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month and begins Unleavened Bread on the fifteenth for seven days. It commands unleavened bread, offerings, assemblies, and release from regular work, but does not retell the exodus story here.

questions.question: What happens at the two harvest presentations?
questions.answer: At the first, a priest waves the first sheaf and an animal, grain, and drink offering accompany it before anyone eats the new grain. After counting fifty days, two leavened loaves and a larger group of animal offerings are presented, followed by a rest day and holy assembly.

questions.question: Why does the gleaning command interrupt the festival calendar?
questions.answer: It comes immediately after the fifty-day harvest observance and requires field corners and gleanings to remain for poor people and foreigners. The placement prevents a harvest celebration from being separated from access to that harvest for people without land.

questions.question: What does “afflict” or “deny yourselves” require on the Day of Atonement?
questions.answer: The chapter commands self-affliction or self-denial together with complete rest on the tenth day of the seventh month. It fixes the observance from the preceding evening to evening but does not list the particular acts of self-denial in this passage.

questions.question: What consequences are attached to ignoring the Day of Atonement?
questions.answer: A person who refuses self-denial is to be cut off from the people. For working that day, God says, “I will destroy that person from among his people.” These are severe sanctions attached specifically to the Day of Atonement’s required observance.

questions.question: What does the Feast of Booths ask Israel to do and remember?
questions.answer: The people rest, assemble, bring offerings, take branches and fruit, rejoice for seven days, and live in temporary shelters. The chapter says the shelters teach later generations that Yahweh made Israel live in such shelters after bringing them out of Egypt.

questions.question: What distinguishes the trumpet memorial from the Day of Atonement?
questions.answer: The first day of the seventh month is designated a solemn rest, a memorial of blowing trumpets, and a holy assembly. Regular work stops and an offering is brought. The chapter gives these actions without adding the self-denial required on the tenth day.

glossary.def: A proclaimed sacred assembly, commonly paired in this chapter with stopping ordinary work.
A harvest or sacrificial item presented before Yahweh and then assigned according to the offering rules.
The seventh month's tenth day, marked here by assembly, self-denial, offerings, and complete rest.
Booths in which native-born Israelites dwell for seven days to remember the exodus journey.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: The preceding chapter has regulated holy food, acceptable sacrificial animals, and thanksgiving meat, ending with God’s holy name and the exodus. The calendar now locates communal worship in recurring time.

here.text: Weekly Sabbath and annual observances combine rest and assembly with harvest presentations, self-denial, rejoicing, and temporary shelters. The gleaning command preserves food for poor people and foreigners amid the harvest celebrations.

after.text: Chapter 24 moves from the calendar to the lamps and weekly bread in the sanctuary, then recounts a blasphemy case and gives laws about death, injury, and equal treatment of native and foreigner.
